title: How to Slice Pineapple Thin for Grilled Dessert Skewers
meta_description: Learn how to slice pineapple thin for grilled dessert skewers using a mandoline. Get step‑by‑step tips, safety tricks, and the best way to achieve perfect mando
html:
Grilling pineapple on a skewer is a quick way to add caramelized sweetness to any dessert, but the secret to a flawless result is getting those slices ultra‑thin and even. Using a mandoline slicer makes the difference between a handful of uneven, floppy rings and a stack of restaurant‑thin, uniform slices that glide onto a skewer and grill in seconds. Below is a practical guide to creating perfect mandoline pineapple slices for grilling, from selecting the fruit to mastering the tool and finishing with a few serving ideas.

Pick the Right Pineapple and Prepare It for Slicing

The first step is choosing a ripe pineapple. Look for a fragrant crown, a slight give when you press the skin, and a golden‑yellow hue spreading from the base upward. Once you have your fruit, wash it under cool water, then dry it with a clean towel.

Next, trim the top and bottom with a sharp chef’s knife—about a half‑inch off each end. Stand the pineapple upright and slice down the sides to remove the tough outer rind, following the natural curve of the fruit. After the rind is gone, you’ll have a cylindrical core with a smooth surface ready for the mandoline.

Set Up Your Mandoline Slicer for Thin, Even Rings

Adjust the blade on your Mandoline Slicer to the thinnest setting you can comfortably manage—usually around 1 mm for grilling. The adjustable guard on the slicer protects your fingers while allowing the blade to glide smoothly. Before you begin, place a sturdy cutting board underneath the mandoline and secure it with a damp towel to prevent slipping.

Because pineapple is juicy, you’ll want to keep the work area tidy. Position a bowl or tray directly under the slicer to catch the slices as they fall. If you have a non‑slip mat, place it on the tray for extra stability.

Slice the Pineapple Safely and Efficiently

Hold the pineapple firmly with the hand guard, keeping your fingertips tucked behind the guard’s edge. Push the fruit down the mandoline’s sliding carriage in a slow, steady motion. The blade will produce a continuous ribbon of pineapple; the guard will cut it into neat, even rings.

If you prefer a slightly thicker slice for a softer bite, simply adjust the blade one notch up and repeat. For grilled dessert skewers, aim for the thinnest setting you can handle—those rings will caramelize quickly without turning mushy.

  1. Place the pineapple on the slicer with the guard engaged.
  2. Slide the carriage forward, letting the blade do the work.
  3. Collect the slices in a bowl; pat them dry with a paper towel before threading.

When you’re done, turn off the mandoline, disengage the blade, and carefully wipe it clean with a damp cloth. Store the slicer with the blade covered or in its original case to keep it sharp for future use.

Arrange and Grill the Pineapple Skewers

Thread the mandoline pineapple slices onto metal or bamboo skewers, alternating with other fruit like banana halves or peach wedges if desired. For a simple dessert, just use pineapple alone. Lightly brush each slice with a touch of melted butter or coconut oil; this helps achieve a beautiful caramelized glaze.

Preheat your grill to medium‑high (around 400–425°F). Place the skewers directly over the heat and grill for 1–2 minutes per side. You’ll see the edges turn golden and the natural sugars begin to caramelize. Rotate the skewers gently to avoid burning.

When the pineapple is nicely charred, remove the skewers and let them rest for a minute. Serve them drizzled with a splash of honey, a sprinkle of toasted coconut, or a dollop of vanilla‑bean yogurt for contrast.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Mandoline Slicer

After slicing, the mandoline will be covered in sticky pineapple juice. Rinse the blade under warm water, then use a soft brush or sponge to dislodge any residue. Never submerge the entire slicer if it has wooden handles; instead, wipe the handles with a damp cloth. Dry the mandoline thoroughly before storing to prevent rust.

Periodically inspect the blade for dull spots. A sharp blade not only gives you cleaner slices but also reduces the force needed, making the tool safer to use. If the blade becomes nicked, replace it according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Tips for Perfect Grilled Dessert Skewers

  • Use a dry brush on the slices: Patting the pineapple rings dry before grilling removes excess moisture, leading to quicker caramelization.
  • Don’t overcrowd the grill: Give each skewer space so the heat circulates evenly; this prevents steaming the fruit.
  • Add a splash of citrus: A quick squeeze of lime or orange juice after grilling brightens the sweetness and adds a fresh finish.
  • Experiment with spices: Lightly dust the slices with cinnamon, smoked paprika, or a pinch of sea salt before grilling for an extra flavor dimension.

FAQ

Can I use a regular kitchen knife instead of a mandoline for thin pineapple slices?

You can, but achieving uniform 1 mm thickness with a knife is time‑consuming and risky. A mandoline slicer provides consistent, restaurant‑thin slices in seconds while keeping your fingers protected.

Do I need to peel the pineapple before slicing?

No. After removing the outer rind and the tough core, the fruit’s flesh is ready for the mandoline. The slicer’s guard will handle the remaining skin, leaving you with clean, edible rings.

Is it safe to slice frozen pineapple with a mandoline?

Frozen pineapple is too hard for a mandoline blade and can cause damage or injury. Thaw the fruit first, then slice as described for best results.
